description: Pincoya is a Chiloé water spirit, daughter of Millalobo (king of the sea) and Huenchula. With long blond hair and incomparable beauty, she dances on the shore: facing the sea brings abundant fish, facing the mountains brings scarcity. She and her siblings Pincoy and the Sirena chilota guide drowned sailors to the ghost ship Caleuche.
source: Chiloé oral tradition; Martínez Vilches, Chiloe Misterioso; Bacigalupo, Shamans of the Foye Tree
research_notes: Well-documented in Chilote mythology. The input description correctly identifies her as Millalobo's daughter who influences fishing. No corrections needed.

description: Pishtaco (Quechua: ñakaq; Aymara: kharisiri) is an Andean fat-extracting bogeyman from Peru and Bolivia. Originating in 16th-century conquistador corpse-fat practices, it evolved through priest rumors (nakaq), hacendados, and modern machinery-greasing variants. Victims are waylaid; fat harvested for bells, cosmetics, lubricants. Protection: wayruru beans, garlic, chancaca.
source: Weismantel, Cholas and Pishtacos (2001); Canessa, 'Kharisiri' (2000); Oliver-Smith (1969); Andean oral tradition
research_notes: Well-attested across Quechua and Aymara regions. The input correctly identifies Bolivia but the figure is pan-Andean (Peru/Bolivia). Corrected 'vampire' classification to fat-extractor/cannibal bogeyman per Weismantel.

description: Piuchen (Mapuche: piwichen, 'dry people') is a Chilote/Mapuche vampiric winged serpent. It flies at night sucking blood from humans and livestock, emitting a deadly whistle or paralyzing gaze. In old age it transforms into a bird or frog-like form. Dwells in alerce forests; tracked by bloody urine trails. Killed by plugging its hollow and burning. Linked to vampire bat (Desmodus rotundus).
source: Guevara, Psicolojía del pueblo araucano (1908); Vicuña Cifuentes, Mitos y supersticiones (1915); Pérez, Mitos y leyendas de Chile (2004); Latcham, Lenz, Molina
research_notes: Well-documented in Mapuche and Chilote sources. The input's 'vampire bird' is partially correct but primary form is winged serpent. Added Mapuche etymology and fauna identification.

description: Pombero (Guaraní: Pombéro, Karai Pyhare 'Lord of the Night') is a Guaraní forest spirit of Paraguay, NE Argentina, and S Brazil. Short, ugly, hairy-footed, moves silently, mimics birds, protects birds from children. Mischievous: releases cattle, steals eggs/honey, frightens horses. Appeased with cigars, rum, honey; then guards property. Linked to unexplained pregnancies.
source: Colmán, Nuestros antepasados (1929); Cadogan, 'Animal and Plant Cults in Guarani Lore' (1966); Guaraní oral tradition across Paraguay/Argentina/Brazil
research_notes: Well-attested Guaraní being across three countries. The input correctly describes appearance/behavior. Both Uruguay and Argentina entries refer to the same Guaraní cultural figure; no correction needed beyond noting shared cultural region.

description: The puma (kay pacha) is one of three sacred animals of the Inca Trilogy, representing the earthly world (Kay Pacha) with condor (sky) and serpent (underworld). Associated with Inti the sun god, the puma symbolizes strength, vitality, sovereignty. Inca emperor was sun-descended; puma imagery shaped Cusco's layout and royal textiles. A cosmological emblem, not a named spirit.
source: Inca mythology; Huarochirí Manuscript; Urton, Inca Myths; Zuidema, 'Inca Civilization in Cuzco'
research_notes: Well-attested as cosmological symbol, not an independent named spirit. The input treats it as a 'spirit' but it is properly the sacred animal representing Kay Pacha. Corrected classification from 'forest-spirit' to cosmological emblem.

description: Camahueto is a Chilote aquatic bull from Chiloé Archipelago, Chile. Born in rivers with a single spiral horn like a unicorn, it grows massive and migrates to the sea. Destructive on land: destroys crops, creates valleys and floods. Only a machi can lasso it with kelp and return it to the ocean. Its horn shavings are prized medicine.
source: Chilote mythology; Chamberlain, J. American Folklore (1910); Windh, Vancouver Sun (2006); Chiloé oral tradition
research_notes: Well-attested Chilote creature. Input correctly identifies as aquatic bull. Added details: river birth, sea migration, machi's kelp lasso, horn as medicine.

description: Ole Higue (Ol' Higue) is a Guyanese/Caribbean vampire-witch from West African soucouyant traditions. By day an elderly woman; by night she sheds skin (stored in a calabash), becomes a fiery flying orb, and sucks blood from infants. Explains infant mortality. Repelled by scattering rice/salt (must count grains), hot pepper sauce, or finding her hidden skin. Part of Caribbean jumbie/duppy complex.
source: Beckwith, Black Roadways (1929); Duppy/Soucouyant studies (Jamaica, Trinidad, Guyana); Leach, Jamaican Duppy Lore (1961); Guyanese oral tradition
research_notes: Well-attested across Caribbean (Soucouyant/Old Higue). The input correctly identifies Guyana and shapeshifting behavior. Corrected 'spirit' classification to vampire-witch; added skin-shedding and rice-counting protection details.

description: Nahuelito is a Patagonian lake monster of Nahuel Huapi Lake, Argentina. First reported 1897 by Dr. Onelli; 1910 Garret sighting (5-7m serpent). 1960 Navy 18-day sonar pursuit. 1988 photos in Río Negro newspaper. Described as giant serpent, huge hump, or plesiosaur. Name from Mapuche 'nahuel' (jaguar). Indigenous antecedents likely; cryptozoological status unresolved.

research_notes: Well-attested as cryptozoological/folklore entity. Input correctly identifies location and serpent/hump descriptions. Added historical sightings timeline and Mapuche etymology.

Represent consequences of breaking admapu (cosmic law). Central to Mapuche spiritual warfare.
